paragraphs: This paper studies when a nonnegative matrix can be expressed through two smaller nonnegative matrices in the structured form Ω = ZPZ′. The original matrix has rank K, so the proposed representation also uses K dimensions. The central complication is that a matrix with nonnegative entries can still have negative eigenvalues. Most earlier work considered the case without negative eigenvalues; this paper addresses a general number of them.

The authors develop new proofs giving sharp results about when this factorization is possible. This matters because a structured factorization can connect a mathematical matrix description to an interpretable model. The result extends the range of matrices covered by existing theory, rather than merely offering another numerical procedure for seeking a factorization.

The application concerns networks with K communities. The authors use their factorization results to determine when a rank-K network model can be rewritten as the interpretable DCMM model. They establish that this rewriting is always possible within the parameter range they identify as especially relevant. That conclusion applies to the stated range, rather than every conceivable rank-K network model.
neurips-2022-a-sharp-nmf-result-with-app.tldr: Sharp nonnegative matrix factorization results show when rank-K network models can be rewritten as interpretable DCMM models.

paragraphs: Deleting a training record does not automatically remove its influence from a trained model. This paper studies approximate removal for learning algorithms that return an empirical risk minimizer: a model minimizing the training objective. It focuses on deletion requests arriving over time, so the removal method must support an ongoing sequence of updates.

The authors develop an online algorithm using the infinitesimal jackknife to approximate the effect of removing data. A distinguishing feature is support for objectives with nonsmooth regularizers, including ℓ1, elastic net, and nuclear norm penalties. They provide guarantees concerning unlearning, generalization, and deletion capacity that are consistent with leading methods. Benchmark experiments report faster execution than prior approaches while retaining the same memory requirements and test accuracy.

The paper also establishes a limitation involving model selection. It proves that all approximate unlearning algorithms introduced up to this work fail in problem settings where common hyperparameter tuning procedures, such as cross-validation, selected the model. The finding makes the model-selection stage part of the removal problem, beyond updating the final fitted parameters.
neurips-2022-algorithms-that-approximate.tldr: An efficient online unlearning method handles nonsmooth regularization, while a separate result exposes failures when model selection used common hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: This paper asks what information about a computer program the human brain represents while someone understands it. The authors analyze functional magnetic resonance imaging recordings from programmers reading Python code. They examine both static properties, such as aspects of a program's syntax tree, and dynamic properties related to what happens when the program runs.

To investigate finer details, the authors train a probe that aligns the brain recordings with representations produced by several machine learning models of code. This comparison asks whether information in the measured brain activity corresponds to information captured by artificial models. It complements the analysis of individual code properties by examining richer learned representations.

The results identify code-related information in both the Multiple Demand and Language systems, despite their different cognitive roles. Both systems encode particular program properties and show distinct alignments with machine-learned representations. The authors interpret this as evidence suggesting at least two neural mechanisms involved in understanding and evaluating programs. They also argue that these findings motivate code-model training objectives extending beyond static language modeling.
neurips-2022-convergent-representations-.tldr: Brain recordings reveal distinct code representations in two cognitive systems, with alignments to representations learned by machine learning models.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories to image regions, but transferring a model between image domains becomes difficult when their geometry differs. This paper addresses unknown optical distortion between source and target images. It highlights a gap in adaptation research: changes in lighting and texture have received much more attention than changes in how a lens bends the scene.

The proposed DaDA framework learns relative distortion through diffeomorphic transformations, allowing it to model detailed geometric deformation between domains. The authors also show that adding global affine transformations to the already deformed source images improves adaptation further. These two components address fine-grained deformation and broader geometric changes within the same framework.

The authors introduce benchmarks transferring from rectilinear source images to fisheye target images without target supervision. Experiments report advantages over leading methods under unknown relative distortion. They additionally find that distortion-aware adaptation improves the initial models and pseudo labels used for self-supervised learning. Thus, the geometric adaptation contributes both directly to segmentation and to the quality of the model-generated supervision used afterward.
neurips-2022-dada-distortion-aware-domai.tldr: DaDA improves unsupervised segmentation transfer by learning geometric distortions between source and target images.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why transformers can learn from examples supplied in their current context without being explicitly trained for that ability. It examines the training data distribution as a source of this behavior. The experiments identify burstiness, where items occur in clusters, and large numbers of rare classes as properties that encourage in-context learning.

The behavior becomes stronger when an item's meaning or interpretation can change. These properties resemble naturalistic data, including language, and differ from the uniform, independently sampled distributions often used in supervised learning. The findings connect adaptation within a context to regularities encountered during training, rather than treating the ability as a consequence of architecture alone.

Initial experiments found a trade-off between in-context learning and learning stored in model weights. Later experiments showed that both could coexist under a skewed Zipfian training distribution. In further comparisons, the tested naturalistic distributions elicited in-context learning in transformers but not recurrent models. Together, these results point to an interaction between architecture and data distribution, and suggest ways to encourage both learning modes beyond language.
neurips-2022-data-distributional-propert.tldr: Experiments show that particular training-data distributions encourage transformer in-context learning and can allow it to coexist with learning stored in weights.

paragraphs: Few-shot detection and instance segmentation require models to recognize new object classes from only a few labeled instances. This paper identifies missing labels as a source of biased classification in that setting. When an object lacks a label, it can contribute a misleading negative training example, even though it should not be treated as evidence against recognizing the object.

The authors' analysis motivates splitting the usual classification head into two heads. These separately handle clear positive examples and noisy negatives arising from missing labels. The purpose is to let the model learn new classes while reducing interference from incorrect negative supervision. The proposed change reorganizes the classifier without adding parameters or computational cost, according to the abstract.

Experiments evaluate the method on PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO for both few-shot object detection and instance segmentation. The authors report consistent, large improvements over their baseline and leading methods. The contribution links a specific supervision problem to a simple architectural response: distinguishing reliable positive evidence from negative evidence that may be corrupted by incomplete annotation.
neurips-2022-decoupling-classifier-for-b.tldr: Splitting the classifier into two heads reduces bias from missing labels and improves few-shot detection and instance segmentation without added computation or parameters.

paragraphs: This paper develops efficient statistical tests for three questions: whether two samples come from the same distribution, whether variables are independent, and whether data fit a proposed distribution. The methods use MMD, HSIC, and KSD, respectively. Their incomplete U-statistics allow computation to vary between linear and quadratic cost in the number of samples.

Each test combines several kernel bandwidths, enabling it to detect differences at multiple scales. This addresses kernel selection without requiring one bandwidth to capture every relevant departure from the null hypothesis. The authors show that many bandwidths can be aggregated without a significant loss of test power, and derive a bound supporting thresholds obtained through wild bootstrap.

For the two-sample and independence tests, the theory quantifies the trade-off between computation and detectable departures. At quadratic cost, wild bootstrap matches the minimax optimal rates of permutation-based approaches and oracle quantiles. Numerical experiments examine the efficiency–power trade-off. Across all three testing problems, the proposed linear-time methods outperform existing linear-time tests or at least match their power.
neurips-2022-efficient-aggregated-kernel.tldr: Aggregating kernel tests built from incomplete U-statistics provides adjustable computational cost with theoretical and empirical support for their detection power.

paragraphs: Variational quantum circuits learn by adjusting circuit parameters, but this becomes difficult when the gradients guiding those adjustments become extremely small. The paper addresses the barren plateau problem, in which gradients can shrink exponentially as circuit depth and the number of qubits increase. This behavior has contributed to doubts about the practical trainability of deep quantum circuits.

The authors propose initializing the parameters with appropriately chosen Gaussian distributions. Under this initialization, they prove that the gradient norm decreases at most polynomially as depth and qubit count grow. The choice of initialization is therefore central to the guarantee: the result does not say that arbitrary random initial parameters avoid exponentially small gradients.

The theory covers both local and global observables, including the global case previously believed to suffer vanishing gradients even in very shallow circuits. Experiments in quantum simulation and quantum chemistry support the theoretical findings. The contribution challenges the idea that depth itself makes these circuits impractical by showing that a suitable starting parameter distribution can substantially change how the gradient scales.
neurips-2022-escaping-from-the-barren-pl.tldr: Proper Gaussian initialization provably prevents gradient norms from decaying faster than polynomially as quantum circuits become deeper and contain more qubits.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents often receive intrinsic rewards that encourage exploration even when task rewards are hard to find. Existing approaches may reward unfamiliar observations or difficulty predicting what happens next. This paper addresses a problem with applying those signals in partially observable environments: the exploration reward can fade before the agent has explored effectively.

The proposed RC-GVF method builds intrinsic rewards from predictions of temporally extended general value functions. Its exploration signal therefore draws on predictions spanning time, rather than only the novelty of the present observation or errors in predicting precise environment dynamics. The approach connects novelty-based exploration and artificial curiosity through this broader prediction task.

Experiments show improved exploration in a difficult diabolical lock problem. In partially observable MiniGrid environments, RC-GVF substantially outperforms previous methods when ground-truth episodic counts are unavailable. Giving the agent panoramic observations improves results further, making it competitive with baselines that receive privileged episodic-count information. These comparisons show how the method performs under different information conditions, with the strongest reported comparison also using richer observations.
neurips-2022-exploring-through-random-cu.tldr: RC-GVF uses predictions extending over time to generate curiosity rewards that improve exploration in tested partially observable environments.

paragraphs: When several reinforcement learning agents learn simultaneously, each agent faces an environment that changes as the others update their behavior. One response is to anticipate those updates and act in ways that influence other agents' future policies. This paper argues that looking ahead through only a finite number of updates can favor temporary outcomes rather than desirable long-term behavior.

The authors introduce an objective that considers the limiting policies of other agents as time approaches infinity. Each agent seeks to maximize its average reward while accounting directly for how its own behavior affects the set of policies the others converge to. This makes influence over eventual outcomes part of the optimization target.

The paper characterizes desirable solution concepts for this setting and develops practical ways to optimize over possible outcomes. Across a diverse collection of multiagent benchmarks, the resulting approach achieves better long-term performance than leading baselines. The contribution is a framework for reasoning about influence at convergence, supported by experiments showing advantages from that longer perspective in the evaluated domains.
neurips-2022-influencing-long-term-behav.tldr: A multiagent learning objective accounts for other agents' limiting policies and improves long-term performance on evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Processing very large batches can accelerate training, but object detection and segmentation models can lose substantial performance in that regime. This paper identifies a problem involving their multiple components: gradient variances can become misaligned across the backbone, feature pyramid, and prediction heads. The authors show that this mismatch can cause large-batch training to fail.

Their Adaptive Gradient Variance Modulator, or AGVM, aligns these variances across modules. It is designed to work with different architectures, including convolutional networks and transformers, and with optimizers such as SGD and AdamW. The paper also provides theoretical analysis and evaluates detection and several forms of segmentation on COCO and ADE20K.

The experiments report more stable generalization than previous approaches at batch sizes as large as 10,000. One configuration trains Faster R-CNN with ResNet50 in 4.2 minutes without losing performance. A billion-parameter detector trains in 3.5 hours, a reported 20.9-fold reduction, while achieving 62.2 mAP on COCO. These results demonstrate the practical value of coordinating optimization across a predictor's different modules.
neurips-2022-large-batch-optimization-fo.tldr: AGVM aligns gradient variances across detection and segmentation modules, enabling very large batches and substantially faster training in reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a training method for neural networks whose sensitivity to input changes is constrained. Such Lipschitz bounds support certified robustness: guarantees concerning perturbations within a specified size. The proposed layer-wise orthogonal training method, LOT, targets convolutional layers with a Lipschitz bound of one, using an unconstrained matrix to parameterize an orthogonal matrix.

A central computational step is obtaining an inverse square root associated with the convolution kernel. LOT performs this efficiently by moving to the Fourier frequency domain. The paper also connects semi-supervised learning to formal robustness guarantees, proving that it improves certified robustness for Lipschitz-bounded models rather than addressing only empirical resistance to attacks.

Evaluations report improved deterministic ℓ2 certified robustness and successful scaling to deeper networks. For supervised 40-layer networks at radius 36/255, the reported values rise from 59.04% to 63.50% on CIFAR-10 and from 32.57% to 34.59% on CIFAR-100. With unlabeled data, CIFAR-10 robustness at radius 108/255 increases from 36.04% to 42.39%. LOT also outperforms the evaluated baselines while using one-third of their evaluation time.
neurips-2022-lot-layer-wise-orthogonal-t.tldr: LOT efficiently trains Lipschitz-constrained convolutional networks and improves reported certified robustness, with further gains from semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Iterative magnitude pruning can discover sparse subnetworks that train to the accuracy of a dense network after a short period of dense training. The same behavior does not hold at random initialization. This paper investigates what that early training phase contributes, examining both the data used during pretraining and the geometry of the loss landscape.

The experiments show that, when the number of pretraining iterations stays fixed, a small randomly selected fraction of the data can produce an equally good initialization for pruning. Selecting only easy training examples can further reduce the number of steps needed, compared with using either the full dataset or a random subset. These findings distinguish the amount of data encountered from the number and character of early updates.

The authors also identify loss-landscape properties predictive of pruning performance. In particular, a greater number of examples exhibiting linear mode connectivity in the dense network correlates with better initializations. This is evidence of an association, rather than a claim that the geometric property alone causes successful pruning. Together, the observations clarify how early training prepares a network for sparsification.
neurips-2022-lottery-tickets-on-a-data-d.tldr: Experiments show that small data subsets can prepare networks for successful pruning, while easy examples can reduce the required pretraining steps.

paragraphs: The strong lottery ticket hypothesis concerns whether a randomly initialized neural network already contains a subnetwork that approximates a desired target network. This perspective makes pruning a way to reveal useful computation already present in the initial weights. A central theoretical question is how much larger the random network must be for such a subnetwork to exist.

For ReLU networks, earlier results established that a target of depth L could be approximated inside a random network of depth 2L with a logarithmic increase in width. This paper improves the sufficient depth to L+1 while retaining logarithmic overparameterization. Only one additional layer is needed in the new construction, bringing the depth requirement closer to architectures commonly used in practice.

The authors' construction also applies to a large class of activation functions, extending beyond ReLU. The result broadens the theoretical settings in which suitable subnetworks can exist without substantial extra depth. Its main contribution is an existence and approximation result: it establishes sufficient network size for lottery tickets, rather than reporting that any particular practical pruning procedure will reliably find them.
neurips-2022-most-activation-functions-c.tldr: A new construction shows that depth L+1 can suffice to contain lottery-ticket approximations of depth-L networks, with logarithmic overparameterization and broad activation support.

paragraphs: Facial expression recognition can become entangled with facial identity: a model may rely on who a person is while interpreting their expression. This paper addresses variation between identities by seeking pairs of people displaying similar expressions. Such matches provide a way to quantify how expression-related features differ across individuals.

The authors formulate matching as an optimal transport problem. Similarity between features defines the transportation cost, and Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration finds a flow minimizing that cost. The resulting correspondence connects similar expressions across different identities. This supplies an explicit mechanism for addressing identity variation within expression recognition, rather than leaving that relationship implicit in the learned representation.

The matching component can be added to other models, and the authors describe its computational overhead as acceptable. Experiments on in-the-wild datasets report improvements in PCC and CCC, with gains described as reaching around 10% or more relative to the runner-up. These findings support the usefulness of cross-identity matching for the evaluated recognition tasks; the reported gains concern those performance measures and experimental comparisons.
neurips-2022-optimal-transport-based-ide.tldr: Optimal transport matches similar expressions across identities, helping facial expression models address identity variation and improve reported recognition performance.

paragraphs: A backdoored convolutional network can behave normally on ordinary inputs while responding to a trigger with an attacker-chosen behavior. Such backdoors can be introduced through a small proportion of poisoned training samples. This paper seeks to locate the neurons involved by examining their pre-activation distributions, meaning the values entering their activation functions.

The authors find that benign and poisoned inputs produce substantially different statistical moments for backdoor neurons. They show this distinguishing property to be attack-invariant. Based on assumptions about neuron activation distributions, they develop two detection strategies: one uses differential entropy, while the other uses Kullback-Leibler divergence between a benign distribution and a hypothetical distribution constructed from poisoned-data statistics.

The approach turns internal distributional behavior into evidence for identifying backdoor neurons. Its detection strategies rely on the stated distributional assumptions, rather than following from the moment differences alone. Experiments report that both defenses are computationally efficient and effective against various backdoor attacks. The findings support statistical inspection of pre-activations as a practical route to locating the internal components associated with trigger behavior.
neurips-2022-pre-activation-distribution.tldr: Differences in neuron pre-activation distributions motivate two efficient backdoor detection strategies supported by experiments across various attacks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a small public dataset can help estimate a distribution while protecting private data through differential privacy. For a d-dimensional Gaussian, the public examples may come from another Gaussian with extremely little similarity in total variation distance. Even under that mismatch, d+1 public samples suffice to remove dependence on distribution range parameters from the private sample requirement under pure or concentrated privacy.

The authors also examine separated Gaussian mixtures, where they assume the public and private data follow the same distribution. With a public sample amount independent of dimension, they obtain a polynomial improvement in the private sample requirement as a function of the number of mixture components. Under approximate privacy, this setting also removes dependence on range parameters.

When the public sample amount grows linearly with dimension, range dependence can be removed even under concentrated privacy, alongside further improvements in overall sample complexity. These results distinguish the benefits available under different privacy definitions and public-data budgets. They establish sufficient amounts of public data, with different distributional assumptions for single Gaussians and mixtures.
neurips-2022-private-estimation-with-pub.tldr: Small public datasets can remove range-dependent private sample requirements for Gaussian estimation and improve private estimation of separated Gaussian mixtures.

paragraphs: Image generators built to produce high-quality pictures are poorly matched to editing the low-quality images commonly encountered outside curated datasets. An input may already contain blur, noise, or compression artifacts, and editing its content need not require changing that quality. This paper introduces QC-StyleGAN to make image quality an explicit control within the generator.

The proposed network uses a quality control code to synthesize different degradations or recover a sharp image. Combined with GAN inversion and manipulation techniques, it can edit low-quality inputs while preserving their quality. This makes quality a controllable property of generation and manipulation, rather than requiring all outputs to conform to a high-quality appearance.

The same structure also provides image restoration for noise, blur, compression artifacts, and mixtures of these degradations. The authors demonstrate additional applications involving the synthesis, transfer, and interpolation of degradation. These uses follow from representing quality within the generative model: it can preserve an existing degraded appearance during an edit, change that appearance deliberately, or move toward a restored output.
neurips-2022-qc-stylegan-quality-control.tldr: QC-StyleGAN adds explicit quality control, allowing low-quality image editing, degradation manipulation, and restoration within one generative framework.

paragraphs: Gradient boosting decision tree training commonly represents gradients and related statistics with high-precision floating-point numbers. This paper asks how much precision those gradients actually need. The authors introduce a simple quantization method that replaces high-precision gradient representations with much lower-precision values during training.

Their theoretical analysis and experiments show that gradients can require as few as two or three bits without reducing performance in the studied settings. With these representations, most arithmetic operations can use 8-, 16-, or 32-bit integers. This creates opportunities to accelerate histogram statistics and reduce the communication required to exchange statistical information during distributed training.

Benchmarks on CPUs, GPUs, and distributed clusters show speedups of up to twofold over leading gradient boosting systems across the evaluated datasets. The authors also identify low-precision hardware as a potential avenue for further efficiency. The observed speedups establish a practical benefit of the quantization strategy, while the hardware discussion points to possible future gains rather than additional measured results.
neurips-2022-quantized-training-of-gradi.tldr: Very low-precision gradients can preserve gradient boosting performance in studied settings while enabling reported training speedups of up to twofold.

paragraphs: Architecture search often designs a network for one task and one hardware platform. In few-shot learning, however, many tasks may need deployment across many different devices. Running a separate search for every combination creates a task-count times hardware-count scaling problem. This paper targets that repeated search burden.

The proposed H-Meta-NAS method integrates Model Agnostic Meta Learning into hardware-aware architecture search. Its goal is to adapt architectures rapidly to new tasks while accounting for deployment constraints. Meta-learning provides the framework for adaptation across tasks, and hardware awareness makes the target platform part of the optimization rather than a consideration added after architecture selection.

On popular few-shot benchmarks with several hardware platforms and constraints, the authors report Pareto dominance over a variety of searched and manually designed baselines. On the five-way, one-shot Mini-ImageNet task, they report an accuracy advantage of 5.21% over the best manual baseline while using 60% less computation. These findings support adapting architectures across task and hardware combinations as a way to improve both predictive performance and computational requirements.
neurips-2022-rapid-model-architecture-ad.tldr: H-Meta-NAS combines meta-learning with hardware-aware architecture search to adapt networks across few-shot tasks and deployment platforms.

paragraphs: This paper studies predicting a tree's root value from observations at its leaves when values propagate through a Markov process. Belief propagation achieves Bayes-optimal reconstruction in this setting. The authors ask how well low-degree polynomials perform, because this class of methods is often used to assess the difficulty of statistical computation.

They construct simple bounded-arity tree models with N leaves where an efficient algorithm achieves nontrivial, noise-robust reconstruction, but polynomials of degree N^c cannot, for a positive constant determined by the arity. They establish another separation when the tree is unknown and multiple samples have correlated root assignments: a simple Statistical Query algorithm succeeds while polynomials at that degree fail.

These examples demonstrate limitations of using low-degree polynomial performance to represent what polynomial-time algorithms can achieve in Bayesian estimation. A further consequence concerns RBF kernel ridge regression: on the constructed problem, it requires exp(N^c′) samples to obtain nontrivial correlation with the true regression function, for a positive arity-dependent constant. The results provide specific separations between computational approaches within tree reconstruction.
neurips-2022-reconstruction-on-trees-and.tldr: Constructed tree models permit efficient root reconstruction while defeating low-degree polynomials and requiring extremely many samples for RBF kernel ridge regression.

paragraphs: A molecular graph describes chemical connectivity, but discovering favorable three-dimensional shapes requires searching a large space of possible conformations. This paper introduces RMCF to generate diverse, low-energy conformations by sampling a learned molecular conformation field. Its approach reduces the complexity of describing each molecule before learning how its parts fit together.

A data-driven segmentation algorithm partitions the molecule into structural building blocks, reducing the number of degrees of freedom the model must handle. A Markov Random Field then learns the joint distribution of fragment configurations and the dihedral angles connecting fragments. Modeling these quantities jointly allows sampling to reach different low-energy regions while accounting for relationships across the molecule.

On the GEOM-Drugs conformation-generation task, the authors report consistent improvements over leading models. They attribute the gains to the regularized feature space and the global distribution over fragment configurations. The method therefore combines a reduced representation with coordinated sampling of molecular parts. The authors suggest that it could extend to larger biomolecular systems, presenting that extension as a possibility rather than an established experimental result.
neurips-2022-regularized-molecular-confo.tldr: RMCF generates diverse low-energy molecular shapes by learning a joint distribution over structural fragments and the angles connecting them.

paragraphs: Discharge instructions help patients and carers manage conditions outside hospital, but preparing complete and accurate instructions takes clinicians time. This paper introduces automatic patient-instruction generation as a task and builds a clinical benchmark dataset. The intended output is a draft that a clinician can review, modify, and approve, keeping clinical judgment within the workflow.

The proposed Re³Writer follows three stages inspired by physicians' working patterns. It retrieves relevant experience from historical instructions, reasons about related medical knowledge, and refines those sources to extract useful information. That information then supports instructions for a previously unseen patient using their hospitalization records. Retrieval and reasoning thus supply material that is filtered before generation.

Experiments show improvements across all reported metrics for six different models. The largest relative gains are 20% in BLEU-4, 11% in ROUGE-L, and 19% in METEOR. The paper also reports human evaluations assessing usefulness for clinical practice. These findings support the generation framework's measured quality and evaluated usefulness; the work positions the system as assistance for clinician-reviewed discharge documentation.
neurips-2022-retrieve-reason-and-refine-.tldr: Re³Writer combines historical instruction retrieval, medical reasoning, and refinement to improve patient-instruction drafts intended for clinician review.

paragraphs: A hypergraph can represent relationships involving multiple genes at once, making genetic pathways natural hyperedges. This paper focuses on predicting properties of subgraphs within such a structure. For example, a patient can be represented by the subset of genes carrying mutations, embedded within a broader network of functional pathways.

SHINE learns representations for both genes and pathways through dual attention message passing. It jointly optimizes subgraph classification and a regularization objective concerning similarities between hypergraph nodes. A subgraph attention layer then aggregates the learned representations, and a multilayer perceptron makes the prediction. This architecture links the patient's selected genes to the functional relationships encoded by pathways.

The authors evaluate SHINE on large-scale sequencing and curated datasets against graph and hypergraph neural networks, XGBoost, nonnegative matrix factorization, and polygenic risk score models. They report significant improvements over every comparison model and disease models offering interpretable functional insights. The contribution extends hypergraph representation learning toward subgraph-level inference, where the object being classified is a biologically meaningful subset of the overall structure.
neurips-2022-shine-subhypergraph-inducti.tldr: SHINE combines gene and pathway representations to classify patient-related subgraphs, improving prediction and providing functional insights in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies discovering classes from unlabeled data across domains whose class proportions change while the distribution within each class stays fixed. It calls this setting Latent Label Shift. The guiding idea is that examples whose prevalence changes together can reveal a shared class, even when similarity in the original feature space suggests misleading groupings.

For finite input spaces, the authors establish an equivalence with topic modeling: inputs act as words, domains as documents, and classes as topics. For continuous inputs, they prove identifiability under an assumption that each class has a separable support region. With oracle access to domain probabilities given an input, class proportions and class probabilities can then be recovered up to renaming the classes.

The practical algorithm trains a domain discriminator, clusters examples in its output space, and applies nonnegative matrix factorization to the discretized data. It combines the recovered quantities with discriminator outputs to obtain class predictions. Semisynthetic experiments show improvements over competitive unsupervised classifiers, including cases where feature-space similarity misrepresents the true grouping. The results make distribution shift a source of information for discovering classes.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-learning-under.tldr: Under stable class-conditional distributions, changing class proportions across domains can help identify unlabeled classes through a connection to topic modeling.
